topic: In a thin layer of Belousov-Zhabotinsky reagent, a broken chemical wave does not heal: its free ends curl into a pair of rotating spirals that keep firing forever.
summary: The Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction is a chemical oscillator. In an unstirred thin layer it behaves as an excitable medium: a disturbance sends out a ring of oxidation that travels at fixed speed, and the medium behind it is briefly refractory. Colliding waves annihilate instead of passing through each other. If a wave is cut, its open ends cannot close and they wind into spiral rotors, which become self-sustaining pacemakers. The Oregonator model reproduces this with an activator and a recovering catalyst.

facts.claim: Boris Belousov observed the oscillating reaction in the early 1950s, and his manuscript reporting it was rejected because reviewers thought it impossible.
Anatol Zhabotinsky took up the reaction as a graduate student in the early 1960s and established its oscillating behaviour.
With the ferroin catalyst the solution swings between red (reduced iron) and blue (oxidised iron), so waves of oxidation are visible as blue bands.
Arthur Winfree reported spiral waves of chemical activity in thin layers of the reagent in Science in 1972.
facts.source_title: Winfree, Spiral waves of chemical activity (Science 175, 1972)

facts.claim: The Oregonator was devised by Field and Noyes in 1974 at the University of Oregon as a reduced model of the Field-Koros-Noyes (FKN) mechanism of the reaction.
In the Oregonator, HBrO2 (X) is the activator species and the oxidised catalyst (Z), whose reduction releases bromide, is the inhibitor species.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Broken wave ends curling into spiral rotors
visualisable_mechanisms.description: A cut wave has two free ends. The ends advance more slowly than the flat front and wind around the refractory core behind them, forming a counter-rotating pair of spirals that become permanent pacemakers.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Erase a short segment of a travelling ring in an Oregonator simulation and let the ends wind up.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Target rings from pacemakers
visualisable_mechanisms.description: A local trigger fires repeatedly, sending concentric rings of oxidation outward at a fixed speed.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Periodic stimuli at a few points in the dish.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Annihilation of colliding waves
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Two waves meeting head-on both stop, because each runs into the refractory tail of the other.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Overlapping ring systems whose fronts cancel along cusped seams.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: Light-inhibited propagation
visualisable_mechanisms.description: In the ruthenium-catalysed variant light produces bromide, so illuminated regions inhibit waves; uneven light makes waves slow or fail.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: A spatially varying inhibitor field with a few strongly inhibited spots acting as obstacles.

open_questions: How does a spiral's core meander in three dimensions when the layer is thick enough for scroll waves?
Why do some spirals drift toward obstacles and anchor there while others wander freely?

surprise.justification: A reaction once rejected as impossible draws the same spirals seen in heart arrhythmias and slime moulds, and a single scratch is enough to start one.
